t: Venus spins slower than it orbits
b: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once on its axis, but only about 225 days to go around the Sun. So one full rotation of Venus lasts longer than its year. It also spins backwards compared with most planets.

q.p: On Venus, which takes longer?

rq.p: About how long does Venus take to spin once?

why: 243 days to rotate beats 225 days to orbit.

b: A neutron star packs more mass than our Sun into a ball about 20 km across. NASA says a sugar-cube-sized lump of its material would weigh around a billion tonnes on Earth.

q.p: A sugar cube of neutron star material would weigh about…

rq.p: Roughly how wide is a neutron star?
o: About as wide as the Sun

why: Atoms are crushed until mostly neutrons remain, packed tight.

b: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth. If the Sun vanished, we would keep seeing it, and orbiting it, for those eight minutes.

q.p: How old is the sunlight hitting you right now?

rq.p: If the Sun vanished, how long until we'd notice?

why: The Sun is about 150 million km away and light covers about 300,000 km each second.

b: To a botanist, a berry is a fleshy fruit grown from one flower with one ovary, usually holding several seeds. Bananas, tomatoes and grapes qualify. Strawberries don't: they grow from a flower's swollen base, and the 'seeds' outside are actually tiny fruits.

q.p: Which of these is a true berry, botanically?

rq.p: What are the 'seeds' on a strawberry's outside?

why: Berry is a botanical category based on how the fruit forms.

t: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood
b: An octopus has two hearts that pump blood through the gills and a third for the rest of the body. Its blood uses a copper-based protein, haemocyanin, to carry oxygen, which turns it blue.

q.p: How many hearts does an octopus have?

rq.p: Why is octopus blood blue?

why: Haemocyanin uses copper; our haemoglobin uses iron.

t: Ice floats because water is weird
b: Most substances are denser as solids. Water expands by about 9% when it freezes, because its molecules lock into an open hexagon pattern. That's why ice floats and lakes freeze from the top down, letting fish survive underneath.

q.p: What happens to water's volume when it freezes?

rq.p: Why do lakes freeze from the top down?
o: Ice is less dense than water
The bottom is warmer from the Sun

why: Hydrogen bonds hold frozen water in a spacious crystal.

t: Saturn is less dense than water
b: Saturn is mostly hydrogen and helium, giving it an average density of about 0.69 grams per cubic centimetre. Water is 1.0. It's the only planet in our solar system less dense than water.

q.p: Which planet is less dense than water?

rq.p: What is Saturn mostly made of?

why: Gas giants are huge but made of light elements.

t: Everest isn't the farthest point from Earth's centre
b: Earth bulges at the equator. Chimborazo in Ecuador is almost on the equator, so its summit is about 2 km farther from Earth's centre than Everest's, even though Everest is far higher above sea level.

q.p: Which summit is farthest from Earth's centre?

rq.p: Why does Chimborazo stick out further?

why: Spinning makes Earth wider around the middle.

b: The earliest shark-like fossils, mainly scales, date back about 450 million years. The first true trees appeared around 385 million years ago. Sharks have outlasted several mass extinctions, including the one that ended the dinosaurs.

q.p: Which came first on Earth?

rq.p: Roughly how long ago did sharks appear?

why: Fossil sharks predate the first forests by tens of millions of years.

b: Tardigrades, or water bears, are animals about half a millimetre long. In 2007 some were sent into orbit and exposed to the vacuum of space. Many survived and later had healthy offspring. They do it by drying out into a dormant state.

q.p: Which animal survived direct exposure to space?

rq.p: How do tardigrades survive extremes?
o: They dry out and go dormant

why: Dormant tardigrades barely metabolise, so they're hard to damage.

b: Honey is very low in water and fairly acidic, and bees add an enzyme that produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide. Microbes struggle to grow in it, so sealed honey can last for years. It may crystallise, but that doesn't mean it has spoiled.

q.p: What usually happens to old sealed honey?
o: It crystallises but is still fine

rq.p: Why do microbes struggle in honey?
o: Too little water and too acidic

why: Sugar draws water out of microbes, drying them out.

t: Babies have more bones than adults
b: A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones, many made partly of cartilage. As the child grows, several fuse together, for example in the skull and the base of the spine. Adults usually end up with 206.

q.p: Who has more bones?

rq.p: How many bones does an adult usually have?

why: Separate infant bones fuse as we grow.

t: Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
b: A lightning bolt heats the air around it to about 30,000 °C in a split second. The visible surface of the Sun is about 5,500 °C. The sudden expansion of that superheated air is what we hear as thunder.

q.p: Which is hotter?

rq.p: What causes thunder?

why: The air in the channel is heated almost instantly and explodes outward.

b: Astronauts left mirrors on the Moon, and scientists bounce lasers off them. These measurements show the Moon moves about 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

q.p: What is the Moon doing, very slowly?

rq.p: How do we measure the Moon's drift?
o: Lasers bounced off mirrors left by astronauts

why: Tides transfer some of Earth's spin energy to the Moon's orbit.

b: The Moon's tides act like a gentle brake on Earth's spin. On average, the day grows longer by roughly 2 milliseconds per century. Hundreds of millions of years ago, a day lasted only about 21 to 22 hours.

q.p: What's slowly happening to the length of Earth's day?

rq.p: What mainly slows Earth's spin?

why: Tidal friction drains a little of Earth's rotation energy.

t: Mars has a volcano 2.5 times Everest
b: Olympus Mons on Mars rises about 22 km, roughly two and a half times the height of Everest above sea level, and spreads about 600 km across. It is one of the largest volcanoes known in the solar system.

q.p: Where is the tallest volcano in our solar system found?

rq.p: About how tall is Olympus Mons?

why: Lower gravity and no moving plates let Martian volcanoes grow huge.

t: A million Earths fit inside the Sun
b: The Sun is about 109 times wider than Earth. Because volume grows with the cube of width, you could fit roughly 1.3 million Earths inside it. The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system.

q.p: Roughly how many Earths could fit inside the Sun?

rq.p: What share of the solar system's mass is in the Sun?

why: 109 times wider means about 109³ ≈ 1.3 million times the volume.

b: Sound is a vibration passing through matter, like air or water. Space is a near-perfect vacuum, so there's almost nothing to carry it. Astronauts talk by radio, which uses light-speed electromagnetic waves that don't need air.

q.p: Could you hear an explosion in space?
o: No, there's nothing to carry sound

rq.p: Why can radio work in space when sound can't?
o: Radio waves don't need matter to travel

why: Sound needs molecules to bump into each other.

t: The coldest known place is a nebula
b: The Boomerang Nebula, about 5,000 light-years away, sits at about 1 degree above absolute zero. That's colder than the faint afterglow of the Big Bang that fills space. Gas rushing out of a dying star cools as it expands.

q.p: Where is the coldest natural place known in the universe?

rq.p: How does the Boomerang Nebula get so cold?
o: Gas cools as it rapidly expands

why: Rapidly expanding gas cools, like spray from an aerosol can.

b: Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, the only animal known to do so. A 2018 study found the last part of their intestine stretches unevenly, with stiffer and stretchier sections that shape the poo into cubes. Wombats use the piles to mark territory.

q.p: Which animal produces cube-shaped poo?

rq.p: What shapes wombat poo into cubes?

why: Different parts of the gut wall stretch differently.

b: In a University of Washington study, researchers wore a particular mask while trapping crows. For years afterwards, crows scolded anyone wearing that mask, including birds that were never trapped. They seemed to learn the face from others.

q.p: What did crows do years after seeing a 'dangerous' mask?

rq.p: How did untrapped crows learn to fear the mask?

why: Crows have excellent memory and share warnings socially.

b: The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs. Males have venomous spurs on their back legs. It hunts underwater with its eyes, ears and nose shut, sensing the tiny electric fields of prey through its bill.

q.p: How does a platypus find food underwater?

rq.p: Which of these is true of the platypus?
o: It's a mammal that lays eggs

why: Its bill has thousands of electroreceptors.

b: Hummingbirds can twist their wings in a figure-eight pattern, getting lift on both the forward and back strokes. That lets them hover in place and fly backwards. No other bird sustains backward flight like that.

q.p: Which bird can fly backwards?

rq.p: What lets hummingbirds hover?

why: Their shoulder joint lets the wing rotate almost fully.

b: A popular myth says glass is a slow liquid, so old windows are thicker at the bottom. In fact, early glassmaking produced uneven panes and builders often set the thick edge downward. At room temperature glass would need far longer than the universe's age to flow visibly.

q.p: Why are some old window panes thicker at the bottom?
o: They were made uneven and fitted that way

rq.p: At room temperature, does glass flow visibly over centuries?

why: Glass is an amorphous solid with no measurable flow at room temperature.

t: Diamond and pencil lead are the same element
b: Diamond and graphite, the 'lead' in pencils, are both pure carbon. In diamond each atom bonds tightly to four neighbours in a rigid 3D network. In graphite, atoms form flat sheets that slide over each other, leaving marks on paper.

q.p: What do diamonds and pencil 'lead' have in common?

rq.p: Why does graphite leave marks on paper?
o: Its sheets of atoms slide off

why: Same atoms, different arrangement, very different properties.
